*"Don't you miss having a strong man to lean on?"* Rebecca223 asked, paying a hundred dollars for the question. *"Would you give up your business if you met the love of your life?"*

Freya decided to answer.

"A business can't replace a man, and a man can't replace your life's work. Though you don't have to please a business the way you do a lover. And the right business will *always* rise to the occasion." Freya smiled. "Which, you have to admit, gives it a clear edge over a man."

The chats exploded. The Twitter and Instagram feeds on her side monitors raced like mad. The feminist community went into overdrive, and the feed suddenly bloomed with colorful-haired avatars like an exotic greenhouse. Now it wasn't even her assistants but Freya's own fans who were reporting and tearing into the right-wingers who had swarmed to the light of her stream from their anonymous loser forums. Right-wingers were always a headache.

Still, three hundred eighty... no, three hundred ninety thousand live viewers were still three hundred ninety thousand viewers. No matter what they smelled like.

Trolls tried to flood the stream with questions like *"Do you swallow?"* and *"Try shaving your legs"*—zero imagination, pure volume. Stupid sad green frogs started popping up in the chat. Freya kept smiling and selectively answering questions, glancing over at her assistants' chat. Like it or not, the comments set the tone. As it turned out, though, she didn't need the moderators' help.

The trolls' moms didn't give them more than five dollars for school lunch. So they were completely crushed by a counterattack from the very core of Freya's audience, who had rallied to the call of her fan groups on Twitter, TikTok, and Instagram. Stay-at-home moms, nail techs, and small-town college girls rushed to their idol's rescue. Housewives who, answering the clarion call of the modern economy, had traded their ladles for oversized smartphones. And then there were the men who craved the attention of all the aforementioned women and started trying to pass as "one of them," never even noticing as they blew twenty bucks a month—or more—on Freya.

Not the best audience if you're a serious woman sharing the secrets of *real* success, sure—but they were loyal. And loyalty counts for a lot in real business.

Right before Freya's eyes, the haters' comments were washed away by twenty- and fifty-dollar messages: *"Go, Freya!", "Freya, we love you!", "#Axelsensexuals!"* The amounts shot up fast, and soon donations under ten dollars weren't even making it onto the screen. At last, she gave a genuine smile.
